item.title: Gang that charged up to Tk 1m, promising jobs abroad, busted
item.description:
The Special Response Battalion (SRB-4) has arrested 12 members of a gang accused of collecting money by promising overseas jobs, work visas and success in examinations. Later, a mobile court sentenced seven of them to varying terms of imprisonment and fined the remaining five.

They were detained during a drive in the capital’s Technical Mor (intersection) area on Friday morning. Later, in the presence of an executive magistrate, seven people were sentenced to imprisonment ranging from seven days to three months.

The convicts are Suruj Mia of Shariatpur; Sabuj of Patuakhali; Shahin of Pabna; Sujon and Shamim of Sirajganj; Abul Bashar, Durjoy and Kaiyum of Kishoreganj; Harun, Riaz and Kamrunnahar of Bhola; and Rezaul Karim of Rangpur.

Lieutenant Colonel Hafizur Rahman, commanding officer of SRB-4, disclosed the information at a press conference at Technical Mor in the capital at noon on Friday.

He said a covert investigation into the gang was conducted following complaints from the Bangladesh-Korea Technical Training Centre (BKTTC) and Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL). After verifying the allegations, the authorities conducted a drive on Friday morning in the presence of a magistrate and brought the suspects to justice.

How the gang operated

According to SRB, the gang assured people aspiring to work abroad that it could arrange work visas at low costs and guarantee that they would pass written examinations. For this, the gang members charged candidates amounts ranging from Tk 40,000 to Tk 1 million, depending on the circumstances. They would then misappropriate the money using various pretexts.

The press conference was told that BOESL, under the Ministry of Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment, recruits workers for overseas employment through government channels. No fees are charged to candidates during the recruitment process. Anyone with a passport can obtain overseas employment opportunities free of charge by taking the required examinations.

These examinations are held every Friday and Saturday at the BKTTC venue. The broker gang primarily targeted candidates who gathered there to sit for the examinations.

BKTTC does not send workers abroad

Lieutenant Colonel Hafizur Rahman said BKTTC is a training centre that offers training in 24 trades of varying durations. Although its certificates can be helpful in securing jobs abroad, the institution does not directly send workers overseas or arrange employment for them.

Therefore, it is important for candidates to understand that receiving training and securing a job are two different things, he said.

SRB has urged people not to make any payments without verification if anyone demands money by guaranteeing overseas employment or success in an examination.

The force said people must verify information through government offices and authorised agencies to avoid fraud. It also advised anyone who falls victim to such scams to inform the authorities promptly.

item.title: Bangladesh squander flying start, reach 317-8 on Day 1
item.description:
Bangladesh compiled 317-8, riding on three half-centuries from openers Tanzid Hasan Tamim, Shadman Islam and wicket-keeper batter Litton Das on Day 1 of the one-off cricket Test against Afghanistan at Sheikh Jayed Stadium in Abu Dhabi, UAE today, Friday.

While the scoreboard suggested an evenly day for the two teams, Bangladesh knew they had squandered a golden chance to bury Afghanistan under an avalanche of runs, specially the kind of start they got through Tanzid.

Tanzid smashed a marauding 71 ball-83, a knock well complemented by his fellow opener Shadman Islam’s 67 and Litton Das’s 53.

Skipper Najmul Hossain Shanto won the toss and opted to bat first, a decision justified well by Taznid who treated Afghan bowlers in disdain, defying the short ball barrage.

Afghanistan employed the short ball tricks, sensing the Bangladesh batters’ weakness against it.

But Tanzid’s aggressive approach kept runs flowing for Bangladesh as the partnership reached 124 runs in no time.

Nonetheless, Afghan pacers didn’t back out from their plan. And their relentless work paid the dividends eventually with Ismat Alam finally got Tanzid with one shorter which the batter edged to the wicket-keeper to be out after hitting eight fours and four sixes.

His dismissal brought Mominul Haque into the crease and he too kept up the rhythm along with Shadman.

After the second-wicket partnership reached 60 runs, Mohammad Saleem got the better of Shadman again with short ball.

Yamin Ahmadzai then dealt a double blow, dismissing Mominul Haque (29) and Mushfiqur Rahim for duck in three balls, leaving Bangladesh at precarious state.

The situation got worsened further when leg-spinner Qais Ahmed got rid of Najmul Hossain Shanto as Bangladesh lost three wickets for 18 balls.

Litton Das and Mehdiy Hasan Miraz repaired the damages with 62 runs for the sixth wicket.

As Bangladesh looked to take the stranglehold again, Ismat Alam came back to take the wicket of Miraz for 24, effectively closing Bangladesh’s path to rack up a healthy total.

Saleem who was the stand out bowler for Afghanistan on Day 1 with 3-70, removed Litton and Hasan Mahmud in five balls to leave Bangladesh eight down.

Bangladesh appeared to be all out but Nayeem Hasan and Taijul Islam made a late resistance, denying Afghanistan further inroads.

Nayeem was batting on 11 with Taijul on 4 at stumps.

item.title: ‘Jamaat secretary general owns 700 auto-rickshaws’: Jamaat seeks evidence from DNCC administrator
item.description:
Referring to Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami Secretary General Mia Golam Porwar, Dhaka North City Corporation (DNCC) Administrator Shafiqul Islam Khan has said an investigation reportedly found that the leader owns 700 auto-rickshaws.

Calling the statement fictional and baseless, Jamaat-e-Islami has demanded evidence to substantiate the claim. If he fails to provide evidence, the party has demanded that the DNCC administrator withdraw his statement and publicly apologise.

Ahsanul Mahboob Zubair, secretary of Jamaat-e-Islami’s central publicity and media department, sent a statement to the media on Friday afternoon protesting the DNCC administrator’s remarks about the party’s secretary general.

The statement titled “Strong condemnation and protest against the DNCC administrator’s irresponsible and baseless statement” said, “We have taken note of a statement made by Dhaka North City Corporation Administrator Shafiqul Islam Khan Milton that the secretary general of a political party owns 700 auto-rickshaws. News published in various media outlets on Friday suggests that his remarks referred to Jamaat-e-Islami Secretary General Mia Golam Porwar. We strongly condemn and protest the dissemination of such fictional, untrue, baseless and fabricated information.”

Earlier in the morning, speaking at the inauguration of the DNCC’s “July Graffiti Remake” programme at the Mirpur-10 roundabout, Shafiqul Islam Khan said political leaders and activists from various parties had been seen participating in the auto-rickshaw movement that day in the name of a protest.

He said there is not a single person in Bangladesh who would take part in a movement in favour of auto-rickshaws. ... The secretary general of a major political party said the government should accept the demands of auto-rickshaw drivers. That is a ridiculous statement. An investigation later reportedly found that the leader owns 700 auto-rickshaws.

The DNCC administrator also remarked that people would not be able to repeatedly change their stance and get away with it.

Criticising Shafiqul Islam’s remarks, Jamaat leader Ahsanul Mahboob Zubair said in the statement that the public expected responsible, fact-based and decent remarks from the DNCC administrator. Before making a serious allegation that a top political leader personally owns 700 auto-rickshaws, it is essential to present specific and reliable evidence, he said.

Making such remarks without publicly presenting credible evidence to support them was not an example of responsible conduct, he added.

The statement said issues related to auto-rickshaw operations, traffic congestion, road discipline and drivers’ livelihoods should be considered in light of reality and the public interest.

Any political party’s statements or positions on these issues should be countered with arguments, facts and practical measures, rather than by making unsubstantiated allegations against a leader, it added.

Calling on the DNCC administrator to publicly present specific and verifiable evidence to support his statement, the statement said, “If he fails to present evidence, we demand that he withdraw his statement and publicly apologise.”

Earlier, on 5 October, Mia Golam Porwar was asked by journalists about the issue after a preparatory meeting of the liaison committee of the 11-party alliance for a long march from Dhaka towards Khulna and Kushtia.

In reply, Mia Golam Porwar said, “I believe the government should accept the demands of auto-rickshaw drivers. None of us should create a situation that leads to instability in the country or gives anyone an opportunity to provoke people.”

The DNCC administrator, Shafiqul Islam Khan, did not mention anyone by name in his remarks. However, for the past several days, several people have claimed on various television talk shows that Jamaat-e-Islami Secretary General Mia Golam Porwar owns 700 auto-rickshaws.

item.title: 11 Bangladeshis among 20 detained in Malaysia over foreign worker quota fraud
item.description:
Malaysia’s Immigration Department (JIM) has detained 20 people, including 11 Bangladeshis, on suspicion of involvement in fraud involving quotas for foreign workers, reports Malaymail, an online news portal of the country.

According to the Malaymail report, they were arrested during a raid in the Taman Datuk Ahmad Razali area on Thursday. The detainees are aged between 23 and 47.

Datuk Zakaria Shaaban, director-general of Malaysia’s Immigration Department, said the operation began at 7.30 am. It was jointly conducted by the Intelligence and Special Operations Division at the department’s headquarters in Putrajaya and two divisions of the Inland Revenue Board (IRB).

He said the raid was carried out based on information provided by members of the public and intelligence gathered by the Immigration Department.

“Those detained comprised two Bangladeshi men believed to be the business owner and manager, six local female employees, and 12 foreign customers—nine Bangladeshi men and three Indonesian women,” Malaymail quoted Zakaria as saying.

In a statement issued today, Friday, Zakaria said the team seized 265 Bangladeshi passports, 63 Indonesian passports, 12 Pakistani passports and one Indian passport. It also seized RM6,700, believed to be money paid by customers.

According to Zakaria, preliminary investigations indicated that the syndicate used a method known as ‘A-to-B’. Under this arrangement, one company, referred to as Employer A, obtained approval to recruit foreign workers and brought them into Malaysia under the Temporary Employment Visit Pass (PLKS).

However, instead of working for their original employer, the workers were supplied to other companies, referred to as Employer B, in exchange for profit.

Zakaria further said that the syndicate was also suspected of submitting false company information to secure foreign worker quota approvals.

Further investigations found that the foreign workers brought into the country did not work for the companies that had applied for the quotas. Instead, they worked independently for other companies.

The Immigration Department director-general said the scheme was believed to generate profits of between RM3,800 and RM5,000 for each worker brought into Malaysia.

To evade taxes, the companies involved allegedly declared profits far below their actual earnings. They also failed to submit records of their personal income for the period from 2020 to 2023.

Zakaria said the Immigration Department would continue to take firm action against all forms of illegal activity, including those who devise, operate and profit from schemes that abuse foreign worker quotas.

item.title: World Mental Health Day
item.description:
More than nine in 10 people in Bangladesh with mental health conditions do not receive treatment, with stigma, inadequate investment and limited access to specialized services contributing to a persistent treatment gap, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
The WHO’s 2025 report, Prevention and management of mental health conditions in Bangladesh: A case for investment, puts the treatment gap at approximately 92% among adults and 95% among children and adolescents.
These estimates are based on the National Mental Health Survey conducted in 2018-19, the latest nationally representative survey cited in the report.
Against this backdrop, Bangladesh observes World Mental Health Day on Friday under the theme “Lived experiences heard: real voices, real change,” which calls for people with lived experience of mental health conditions to help shape the policies and services that affect them.
The 2018-19 survey found that 16.8% of adults and 13.6% of children aged 7-17 had mental health conditions. Among those affected, 92.3% of adults and 94.5% of children had not received treatment.
The findings highlight the scale of the challenge, although they do not represent a new assessment of the country’s mental health situation in 2026.
The WHO’s 2025 report also identifies inadequate financing, a shortage of specialized professionals, limited access to services and medicines, and social stigma as major barriers to care.
According to the report, mental health accounted for just 0.44% of Bangladesh’s total health budget in 2021. Of this expenditure, 67% went to mental hospitals, highlighting the concentration of resources in institutional care rather than prevention and community-based services.
The report estimates that mental, neurological and substance-use conditions cost Bangladesh Tk210.5 billion in 2021, equivalent to around 0.76% of gross domestic product (GDP).
The economic burden includes lost productivity, reduced workforce participation, disability and premature death.
Bangladesh had 260 psychiatrists, or approximately 0.16 per 100,000 people, according to the WHO report.
Psychiatrists and psychiatric nurses were concentrated in and around Dhaka at about five times the rate found in the rest of the country, highlighting the geographic disparity in access to specialized care.
The report identified 69 outpatient and 72 residential mental health facilities nationwide, while noting the absence of community follow-up and day-treatment facilities.
The shortage of accessible services makes regular mental health care difficult for many people outside major cities, particularly those unable to afford private treatment or travel long distances to consult specialists.
In 2025, a WHO-supported programme in Bangladesh provided more than 20,000 mental health consultations, trained 846 non-specialist healthcare providers and conducted 81 supportive supervision visits.
These figures relate specifically to the WHO-supported programme and should not be interpreted as nationwide totals.
The WHO recommends expanding community-based care, integrating mental health services into primary healthcare, strengthening referral systems and medicine supplies, increasing the number of trained professionals, and investing in prevention and early intervention.
The United Nations has also called for mental health systems that respect people’s rights and involve them in decisions about their care.
In his message for World Mental Health Day 2026, UN Secretary-General António Guterres urged governments to “replace exclusion with partnership, and invest in community-centered care.”
“On this day, and every day, let us reaffirm our commitment to mental health, remove stigma and build systems rooted in dignity and rights for all,” he said.
The WHO has echoed the call, urging countries to go beyond simply listening to people with lived experience and ensure they have a meaningful role in shaping mental health policies, services and decisions.

item.title: ‘Mental health awareness remains a major challenge’
item.description:
On the occasion of World Mental Health Day, Professor Dr Saifun Nahar, director of the National Institute of Mental Health and Hospital, spoke to Dhaka Tribune about Bangladesh’s mental health situation, healthcare services, social stigma, mental health among children and adolescents, and suicide prevention.
Dr Saifun Nahar: According to the National Mental Health Survey 2019, the prevalence of mental health problems among adults in Bangladesh is 18.7%, while the rate among children and adolescents is 12.6%. Among people aged 60 and above, 28% experience mental health problems.
Patients with various mental health conditions visit our outpatient and inpatient departments, where we provide treatment for almost all types of mental health problems.
Among children, online gaming addiction, gambling-related problems, internet addiction and mobile phone addiction are becoming increasingly common.
There are different types of mental health problems, which can broadly be classified into neurotic and psychotic disorders. Changes in brain functioning can affect a person's thoughts, emotions, behaviour and daily life.
As a result, their ability to function in their personal, professional, family and social lives may deteriorate. In general, changes in one's daily activities and functioning can help indicate a potential problem.
A mentally healthy person can generally maintain normal functioning and productivity in their work, communication, social interactions and other activities. Significant changes in these areas, however, may indicate a mental health problem.
Many people with psychotic disorders have limited awareness of their condition, and their judgement may also become impaired. Consequently, they may not recognise the need for treatment.
People experiencing neurotic disorders, on the other hand, can often identify changes in themselves. These may include mood swings, a loss of interest in routine activities, difficulty completing tasks or a decline in the quality of their work.
Mental health problems can also manifest as physical symptoms, including loss of appetite, headaches, body aches and digestive problems. They may also affect sexual desire or functioning.
The mind and body are closely connected, and mental health problems can also affect physical health. For example, many patients with depression experience various physical aches and pains. Anxiety-related disorders can cause palpitations, digestive problems and headaches.
Anyone experiencing a mental health problem should seek medical attention. However, when relatives or neighbours learn that someone is receiving mental health treatment, the person may sometimes face social humiliation. We must move away from these superstitions and prejudices. Unless we break this taboo, we will not be able to address the problem effectively.
There are also many misconceptions about mental health. Some people believe that counselling alone is enough to ensure recovery, that medication must be taken for life once treatment begins, that mental illnesses are incurable, or that psychiatric medication damages the brain. We must work to dispel these misconceptions.
Patients can recover with appropriate treatment and medication taken as prescribed by a doctor. We must also strengthen public trust in doctors and mental health services.
More than 500 patients visit our outpatient department every day. Our inpatient department has 400 beds. At times, all the beds are occupied, while on other occasions, occupancy is around 80%.
We are working to improve our services further. The current government is also taking initiatives to advance mental health services.
Our mental health workforce is still inadequate. However, compared with the past, more talented students are choosing to study this subject. We have introduced four additional courses in response to growing interest in the field. At the same time, the workforce is gradually expanding.
Children experience different types of mental health problems depending on their age. Among children and adolescents, we see cases of autism spectrum disorder, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), internet addiction, gaming addiction and mobile phone addiction.
Many children are also developing problematic patterns of pornography use. Drug addiction is another concern among street children, with some becoming increasingly involved in glue sniffing and the use of readily available drugs such as yaba.
A coordinated approach is needed to address mental health problems among children and adolescents. Conflict and other forms of pressure within the family can affect a child's mental well-being. When children regularly witness arguments between their parents, their cognitive development may be affected, and they may develop trust issues later in life.
If they struggle to manage anger and stress, they may also become vulnerable to suicidal thoughts or behaviour.
Similarly, children who experience bullying or humiliation at school, or face excessive academic pressure, may develop various mental health problems that can affect them later in life.
People with certain personality disorders, particularly those with abrasive personality traits, may exhibit suicidal behaviour. People living with various mental illnesses, including those experiencing hallucinations or delusions, may also develop suicidal tendencies. Drug addiction can also increase the risk of suicide.
Awareness is crucial in this regard. Suicide can be prevented by identifying mental health problems early and ensuring that those affected receive appropriate treatment and support.
Mental health services have expanded compared with the situation 10 years ago. Through the World Health Organization's mental health programme, doctors from different districts and upazilas are receiving training to help reduce gaps in treatment services.
Doctors from areas outside major urban centres are brought in for training. After returning to their respective workplaces, they pass on their knowledge and train other healthcare professionals.
There may not be dedicated posts for psychiatrists at district- or upazila-level health complexes. However, doctors working in these areas are being trained to provide primary mental healthcare to patients. After completing their training, they return to their respective areas and provide services there.
Regardless of the cause of an illness, anyone who is unwell should receive appropriate treatment. Whether mental health problems stem from personal circumstances, family issues or other factors, seeking treatment is essential.
Sometimes, people do not realise that they are experiencing a mental health problem. In such cases, family members and relatives should help them seek professional care by taking them to a psychiatrist and arranging the necessary counselling or other treatment.
The government has already undertaken various projects to strengthen community mental health teams. The integration of mental health services into primary healthcare was included in earlier initiatives, and the programme is now being advanced further.
One year is a very short time, and it is not possible to resolve all the challenges within that period. The treatment gap remains substantial. Among adults, it is 92%, while among children, it is 95%.
This means that only 8% of adults who need mental health services are receiving them, while the remaining 92% are not. Among children who need such services, only 5% receive them, leaving 95% without access to the care they need.
If everyone works together, we can bring about positive changes. However, resolving all these problems within a single year is not possible. We are continuing our efforts to improve the situation.
Public awareness remains inadequate, and many people do not give mental health the importance it deserves. Much of the problem can be addressed if people take mental illness seriously and seek treatment when necessary.
Individuals, families, educational institutions and the state must all work together to raise awareness, reduce stigma and ensure that people with mental health conditions receive appropriate care.

item.title: PM says working to bring mental health services to people's doorsteps
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Friday said the government is working to bring mental health services to people's doorsteps by expanding technology-based counselling services and introducing effective referral systems.
“The current government aims to build a healthcare system where mental peace, social security, and the improvement of living standards are given equal importance alongside physical well-being,” he said in a message issued on the eve of World Mental Health Day 2026, which is to be observed on Saturday.
“Embracing this humane perspective, the government is working to bring mental health services to people's doorsteps by expanding the scope of services at the Upazila and primary healthcare levels, developing skilled manpower, establishing effective referral systems, and extending technology-based counseling services,” said the prime minister.
Highlighting the growing importance of mental health as a public health challenge worldwide, he said many people in Bangladesh also suffer from mental health problems but remain deprived of proper treatment and support due to social stigma, lack of awareness, limited access to services and a shortage of skilled professionals.
So, the government has taken various initiatives to improve the accessibility, quality and capacity of mental health services, Tarique Rahman said.
“Initiatives have been taken to establish integrated referral systems at the upazila and district levels and expand tele-counselling services to reach marginalized people,” he said.
The government has also planned to train mental health physicians working at the upazila level, strengthen the capacity of mental health professionals at public hospitals and provide training to a large number of health workers in this field, the prime minister said.
He said the government is also attaching due importance to the mental health of pregnant women, the mental well-being of children and adolescents, and school-based mental health services.
In his message, Tarique said health did not merely mean being physically fit or free from disease, but rather being well physically, mentally, spiritually and socially. So, mental health could not be neglected under any circumstances, he added.
He said protecting mental health was an important component of the government's public welfare-oriented health policy.
Referring to this year's theme, “Lived experiences heard: real voices, real change,” the prime minister said it highlighted the importance of giving due consideration to people's personal experiences, feelings and opinions in mental healthcare. Bangladesh, along with the rest of the world, will observe the day with due importance, he added.
Mental health is not merely a matter of treatment; it is deeply connected with human dignity, family, society and the overall well-being of the state, he said.
Tarique Rahman stressed the need for collective efforts to eliminate fear, shame, superstition and discrimination surrounding mental illness.
“Instead of neglecting or isolating anyone because of their mental health problems, we must listen to them, stand beside them and make access to necessary support easier,” he said.
Listening to the experiences and feelings of people living with mental health conditions and treating them with dignity are prerequisites for bringing about real change, he added.
Addressing mental health professionals, the prime minister urged them to listen attentively to people with sincerity, extend support with empathy and strive to ensure necessary treatment and assistance.
He also stressed the need to raise awareness about mental health among families, educational institutions, the media and people from all walks of life.
Tarique Rahman expressed his belief that collective efforts by the government, healthcare professionals, families, educational institutions and society could help build a healthy Bangladesh where no one would feel hesitant to talk about mental health, ashamed to seek help or feel alone and neglected.
“We want to build a welfare-oriented, safe and humane Bangladesh where every person has the opportunity to lead a healthy and meaningful life with dignity, hope and potential,” he said.
Tarique wished good health and well-being for all people in Bangladesh and around the world on the occasion of World Mental Health Day 2026.

item.title: 6 held, including bank staff, over planned Tk34 lakh robbery
item.description:
Three employees of an Islami Bank agent banking outlet allegedly lost Tk7-8 lakh in online gambling and then misappropriated customers’ money to cover their losses. They later plotted to rob Tk34 lakh belonging to the outlet’s owner and staged a robbery by having a colleague beaten.
Police arrested six people in connection with the incident and recovered Tk1.42 lakh of the looted money, a motorcycle and seven mobile phones.
Naogaon Superintendent of Police Tarikul Islam disclosed the details at a press briefing at his office around 12:30pm on Friday.
The arrested suspects are Swapan, 28, and Hasan Ali, 25, of Bishia village in Raninagar; Islami Bank agent banking officials Sujon, 27, and Abu Taleb, 22; office assistant Russell Babu, 22; and motorcycle owner Rabbi Ali.
According to the SP, agent banking cashier Nazmul and office assistant Russell Babu were carrying Tk34 lakh from Adim Dighirail to the Abadpukur Bazar outlet by motorcycle around noon on October 6.
Around 1pm, a motorcycle intercepted them in front of a Banglalink tower after they crossed Parail Bazar in Raninagar. The attackers allegedly beat them with iron rods and fled with the money.
Police launched an investigation immediately and, using information technology analysis and other intelligence, seized the unregistered motorcycle allegedly used in the robbery and arrested its owner, Rabbi Ali, that night.
Police later arrested Swapan and Hasan Ali in Dinajpur’s Nawabganj on October 7. Based on their information, Sujon, Abu Taleb and Russell Babu were arrested in Raninagar the following day.
During preliminary interrogation, police found that Russell, Sujon and Abu Taleb had been gambling online for several months and lost Tk7-8 lakh. They allegedly withheld customers’ money and used it for gambling.
To cover the losses, they allegedly planned to rob Tk34 lakh belonging to agent banking owner Firoz Hossain. They spent about a month planning the robbery with Swapan, Hasan and others.
As planned, Russell accompanied Nazmul to collect the money and kept the other suspects informed of their location. Once they reached the designated spot, Swapan, Hasan and others allegedly intercepted them, beat them and fled with the money.
Police said Nazmul was the actual victim, while Russell staged the incident and portrayed himself as a victim.
Of the Tk34 lakh, the three agent banking employees were allegedly due to receive Tk10 lakh, while the remaining money was to be divided among the other participants. Swapan and Hasan were initially given Tk1.5 lakh before fleeing to Dinajpur via Joypurhat.
A case has been filed against the accused, who will be sent to jail through court, police said.

item.title: Commerce minister: Calling Ctg Port agreement a ‘sell-out’ is baseless
item.description:
Commerce Minister Khandakar Abdul Muktadir on Friday said the agreement on the New Mooring Container Terminal (NCT) at Chittagong Port was aimed at increasing the terminal’s capacity and efficiency.
He said the agreement was for a fixed term, after which Bangladesh could either renew it or end it.
Describing the deal as “selling out the country” was a cheap and baseless claim, he added.
The minister made the remarks while responding to journalists after an exchange meeting and a grant distribution ceremony organized by Sylhet City Corporation to mark Durga Puja.
The responsibility for operating the NCT, the largest terminal at Chittagong Port, has been given to Dubai-based global terminal operator DP World.
The 15-year concession agreement was formally signed on Thursday, drawing criticism from various quarters.
Replying to questions from journalists, Muktadir said Bangladesh must make its production and export costs competitive with those of other countries to attract foreign investment and new investment from domestic entrepreneurs.
“If the government cannot make Bangladesh competitive in the global market, how can it attract investment?” he asked.
He said the government wanted to improve efficiency at Chittagong Port to achieve this goal, adding that the agreement was signed specifically to improve the country’s operational efficiency.
Muktadir assured that no one currently working at the port would lose their job.
He said improved efficiency would bring greater benefits to workers, including higher remuneration than they currently receive.

item.title: Dengue: One more die, 1,300 hospitalized in 24 hours
item.description:
One more person died of dengue and 1,300 new patients were hospitalized across the country in the 24 hours until 8:00am on Friday.
With the latest death, the dengue death toll has risen to 295 in the country this year, according to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).
The death was reported in Khulna division, it said.
Currently, 5,776 dengue patients are undergoing treatment at hospitals across the country.
Since January 1 this year, a total of 95,451 dengue patients have been admitted to hospitals across the country. Of them, 89,380 have recovered.

item.title: President calls for empathy, awareness to improve mental well-being
item.description:
President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir has urged all to treat people experiencing mental health problems with empathy and respect and underscored the need for ensuring proper mental healthcare and support from families and communities.
"I call for strengthening mental health awareness activities at health centers and educational institutions, alongside public and private initiatives, to ensure the overall mental well-being of all citizens," he said.
In a message issued on Friday ahead of World Mental Health Day 2026, to be observed on Saturday, the President welcomed the initiative to mark the day in Bangladesh, in line with celebrations around the world.
"Mental health is an essential component of overall well-being, working capacity and quality of life," he said, adding that changing global circumstances, economic instability, social unrest, loneliness, drug addiction, family and workplace pressures and other daily challenges are having a profound impact on people's mental health.
"Therefore, mental well-being is as important as physical health," he added.
Describing this year's theme, “Lived Experiences Heard: Real Voices, Real Change,”as timely and significant, the President said it emphasizes the importance of listening to people who directly experience mental health problems and giving due consideration to their perspectives in policymaking and service planning.
The government, he said, had taken various initiatives to bring mental health services closer to people and integrate them into primary healthcare.
The President also highlighted the crucial role of families and communities in identifying mental health problems and ensuring access to appropriate care.
He also underscored the importance of raising public awareness about seeking appropriate medical treatment instead of relying on faith healing or other unscientific practices.
Expressing hope that collective efforts would help build a mentally healthy and productive nation, the President wished success to all programs undertaken to mark World Mental Health Day 2026.

item.title: Tk1.74cr gold haul at Shahjalal Airport: Arman remanded for 5 days
item.description:
A Dhaka court has placed Arman Uddin Siddique on a five-day remand after he was arrested with 1,290 grams of gold paste worth Tk1.74 crore at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport.
Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Hasan Shahadat passed the order on Friday, following a 10-day remand petition filed by the investigation officer, SI Anisur Rahman of Airport Police Station.
SI Abu Bakkar of the Dhaka Metropolitan Police’s prosecution division confirmed the matter.
According to the case documents, Arman arrived in Dhaka from Sharjah on an Air Arabia flight (G9 518) on October 8. Acting on a tip-off, a preventive team of customs officials placed him under surveillance at the airport.
After completing immigration formalities, he was stopped near baggage belt 2 and searched on suspicion.
Customs officials found three oval-shaped packets wrapped in white adhesive tape concealed in his rectum. The packets contained 24-carat gold paste.
According to the National Board of Revenue (NBR), each packet contained 430 grams of gold paste, bringing the total to 1,290 grams. Refining the paste could yield approximately one kilogram of pure gold, with an estimated market value of Tk1.74 crore.
Assistant Revenue Officer HM Mamun Kaisar of Customs filed a case with Airport Police Station under relevant provisions of the Special Powers Act, 1974, and the Customs Act, 2023.
In the remand petition, the investigation officer said Arman had long been involved in gold smuggling by illegally bringing gold into the country from abroad. He said interrogation was necessary to identify and arrest the alleged ringleaders, financiers and absconding accomplices involved in the smuggling network.
After hearing the petition, the court granted a five-day remand.

item.title: Mintoo: Bangladesh to see improved waste management within two years
item.description:
Environment, Forest and Climate Change Minister Abdul Awal Mintoo on Friday said Bangladesh will see significant improvements in waste management across the country within the next one to two years.
He made the remarks while responding to journalists after visiting Gazipur Safari Park on Friday afternoon.
The minister said waste management had not yet been modernised nationwide. A waste-to-energy project had been undertaken in Aminbazar, while work on a waste-to-energy and resource recovery project in Dhaka South had begun. Similar initiatives would be launched in district and upazila towns.
He said pollution could not be effectively addressed without proper waste management, adding that the government was working to bring about the necessary changes. Regarding mismanagement at the safari park, Mintoo said authorities would hold a meeting in Dhaka to hear about the problems and take steps to resolve them.
On the theft of lemurs from the park, he said two lemurs had been stolen and an investigation was underway. He declined to confirm claims that the animals had been taken to Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani's zoo, but assured that strict action would be taken against those found responsible.
Addressing industries established on forest land, the minister said the government could not simply shut down industries given the country's employment needs. Legal action had been taken to recover forest land occupied by existing industries, he added.
He said a meeting involving legal experts and government officials would be held this month to address land-related disputes in Bhawal National Park, including 465 acres reportedly owned by private individuals.

item.title: Commerce Minister: Religious harmony must be preserved as national tradition
item.description:
Commerce, Industries and Textiles and Jute Minister Khandakar Abdul Muktadir on Friday stressed the need to preserve Bangladesh's long-standing tradition of religious harmony, mutual respect and peaceful coexistence among people of all faiths.
"Religious harmony is a unique asset of Bangladesh. Even many large democratic countries around the world cannot demonstrate the kind of religious harmony that Bangladesh enjoys," he said.
The minister made the remarks while speaking as the chief guest at a view exchange meeting and grant distribution program organized on the occasion of the upcoming Sharadiya Durga Puja at the conference room of Sylhet City Corporation (SCC).
At the program, he handed over grants of Tk40,000 each to representatives of 85 Durga Puja mandaps in the city, distributing a total of Tk34 lakh.
Muktadir said the government remained committed to ensuring that people of all religions could celebrate their religious festivals peacefully and without hindrance. He also said the government would work together with all concerned to develop religious institutions.
The minister said he had visited mosques, temples and other religious institutions both before and after being elected as a lawmaker from Sylhet. He added that the SCC administrator was working to address infrastructure-related problems at these institutions, said a ministry press release. He thanked the city corporation authorities for providing financial assistance to the Durga Puja mandaps.
Highlighting the city's development initiatives, Muktadir said development work had been completed on around 550 kilometres of roads out of approximately 800 kilometres across the city corporation's 42 wards.
He said tenders had also been invited for the development of the remaining roads, while initiatives had been taken to begin improvement work on roads under the Roads and Highways Department.
The minister said the authorities had taken initiatives to construct a new bridge over the Surma River beside the historic Keane Bridge. He also said steps were underway to arrange housing for members of the Harijan community.
To address the shortage of safe drinking water in the city, the government had undertaken a major project to treat water from the Chengerkhal and supply it to residents, he added.
Speaking at the program, SCC Administrator Abdul Qayyum Chowdhury said the city corporation, district administration and police administration were working sincerely to ensure the peaceful celebration of Durga Puja. He urged representatives of Puja mandaps and temple committees to contact the city corporation whenever they needed assistance.

item.title: bKash manager shot, Tk3C looted in Sreepur
item.description:
A bKash manager was shot and three sacks containing Tk3 crore were looted after a group of armed robbers intercepted a private car carrying Tk4 crore in Sreepur, Gazipur, on Friday evening. The incident occurred around 6:15pm in Karnapur on the Sreepur-Gosinga road.
Himel Ahmed, 35, an accounts manager for the Sreepur area, was shot in the right side of his abdomen. Three others travelling with him were also injured when the attackers smashed the car windows and assaulted them with Chinese axes.
Himel, son of Mohammad Jasim of Channapara in Sreepur municipality, was initially taken to Sreepur Upazila Health Complex and later referred to Shaheed Tajuddin Ahmad Medical College Hospital in Gazipur for better treatment.
The other injured were Fahad Hossain, 35, a credit manager in the loan division; Rifat, 30, a supervisor for the Sreepur-Mawna area; and private car driver Lal Mia, 32. They received primary treatment.
Fahad said they had collected Tk4 crore from the bKash distribution branch in Narsingdi and were heading towards Mawna in Sreepur around 4:00-4:30pm.
“When we reached Karnapur around 6:15pm, 10-12 motorcycles carrying two people each surrounded our car and blocked our way,” he said.
“Before we could understand what was happening, they smashed the left-side window and shot Himel. They also broke the driver’s window and my door window before attacking us with Chinese axes,” Fahad said.
The attackers then took three of the four cash sacks kept in the rear of the car and fled towards Sreepur within about two minutes. Each sack contained Tk1 crore, he added.
Rafique, proprietor of Channel Enterprise, which operates bKash’s Mawna and Mymensingh’s Bhaluka areas, said the employees were returning after collecting cash from Narsingdi.
He said the robbers surrounded the car near Karnapur and opened fire to create panic before attacking the employees. They then fled with three sacks of cash.
However, Rafique could not immediately confirm the exact amount looted.
Dr Anik Sarker, a physician at Sreepur Upazila Health Complex, said three people were brought to the hospital around 6:30pm.
“Himel had a deep wound on the right side of his abdomen, which appeared to have been caused by a bullet. As his condition deteriorated, he was referred to the Gazipur medical college hospital,” he said.
Sreepur Police Station Officer-in-Charge Mohammad Shahinur Alam said police were investigating the incident and had yet to verify the amount of money allegedly looted.
“The victims told us they were carrying bKash money from Narsingdi when the attackers blocked their vehicle with motorcycles, assaulted them and fled with the cash,” he said.
Police visited the scene immediately after receiving the report and launched an operation to identify and arrest those involved and recover the looted money, the OC added.

item.title: 200 teen gangs with 1,400 members operate in Chittagong
item.description:
At least 200 teen gangs with an estimated 1,400 members operate across Chittagong city, engaging in activities ranging from territorial clashes and drug trading to extortion and land grabbing, according to police records.
The issue has resurfaced following the killing of 16-year-old Hriday in the Taltala area of Wireless Colony under Khulshi police station. Police suspect the murder was linked to a rivalry between two gangs, Five Star and Seven Star.
Police arrested eight teenagers in connection with the killing, which reportedly stemmed from a dispute over seniority and hierarchy. Hriday was a member of Five Star, while the accused teenagers allegedly belonged to Seven Star.
Chittagong Metropolitan Police (CMP) first compiled a list of teen gangs and their alleged leaders in 2019, following the 2018 killing of school student Adnan Isfar in Jamalkhan. The list was updated in March 2024.
According to the list, 119 gangs operate under CMP's North and South zones, while 81 are based in the West and Port zones. Police also identified 64 alleged patrons, including five ward councillors, accused of providing protection or support to the groups.
However, the list has not been comprehensively updated since 2024, leaving uncertainty over the number of active gangs and their current membership.
Several groups reportedly remain active despite political changes after August 5, 2024. These include Bingu and Python in Halishahar, Five Star and Seven Star in Khulshi and Pahartali, Murad and Jasim in Bakalia, Danger in Jamalkhan; and MBS in Muradpur. Other groups have been reported in Panchlaish, Chakbazar and several surrounding neighbourhoods.
Gang members are accused of controlling drug sales, extorting money, grabbing land, regulating roadside vendors and committing snatching. Police sources say some teenagers are also allegedly used as contract killers.
In May 2025, 18-year-old Wahidul Haque, known as Sabbir, died at Chittagong Medical College Hospital after being attacked in Halishahar. Police linked the killing to a feud between Bingu and Python. His father alleged that his son had been killed for refusing to join Python.
Clashes between the Murad and Jasim groups over drug trading and territorial control have also triggered panic in Bakalia. In another incident, teen gang members were reportedly involved in the killing of college student Ashfaq Kabir Sajid, who was allegedly beaten and thrown from the roof of an eight-storey building on April 12.
Chittagong Superintendent of Police Mohammad Masud Alam said operations against teen gangs were continuing across the district, with arrests being made.
CMP Assistant Commissioner for Public Relations Aminur Rashid said police were also targeting those allegedly providing protection to the gangs.
CMP Commissioner Hasan Md Shawkut Ali said police were taking action against teen gangs and other criminals to maintain law and order. “Members of teenage gangs are being brought under the law,” he said.

item.title: Tigers collapse after blazing start
item.description:
Bangladesh squandered a flying start to finish the opening day at 317-8 in 84 overs against Afghanistan in the one-off Test at Sheikh Zayed Stadium in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, on Friday.
The Tigers looked set for a commanding first-day total after their openers put on 124 runs, but Afghanistan fought back with regular wickets to leave the contest finely poised.
Tanzid Hasan Tamim led the charge with a blistering 83 off 71 balls, while Shadman Islam contributed 67. Litton Das provided some resistance later in the innings with a half-century, scoring 53, but Bangladesh lost wickets at regular intervals to surrender their early advantage.
After winning the toss and opting to bat, Bangladesh raced to 134-1 at lunch, scoring at around six runs per over. Tanzid was particularly aggressive, striking eight fours and four sixes to put the Afghan bowlers under pressure.
However, pacer Ismat Alam ended the opening partnership by having Tanzid caught behind, denying him a second Test century. Shadman, who had initially played a supporting role, continued his innings with greater freedom after his partner's departure.
Shadman and Mominul Haque then added 60 runs for the second wicket to keep Bangladesh in control. But Afghanistan's pacers began to exploit Bangladesh's vulnerability against short-pitched deliveries, triggering a dramatic collapse.
Mohammad Saleem broke the partnership by dismissing Shadman, before Yamin Ahmadzai struck twice in quick succession to remove Mominul for 39 and veteran Mushfiqur Rahim for a duck.
The pressure continued to mount as leg-spinner Qais Ahmad dismissed captain Najmul Hossain Shanto for 29, leaving Bangladesh in trouble after a promising start.
Litton and Mehidy Hasan Miraz attempted to steady the innings, but Afghanistan continued to chip away at the lower order.
Saleem finished the day with three wickets, while Ismat claimed two as Afghanistan clawed their way back into the match.
Bangladesh had included an additional spinner, Nayeem Hasan, in their playing XI, anticipating that the pitch would offer greater assistance to spin as the Test progressed.
Despite the late collapse, the Tigers will look to build on Litton's contribution and push towards a more competitive total on the second day.

item.title: First Australia tour for bilateral series begins with defeat
item.description:
Bangladesh women's cricket team failed to make their first-ever ODI in a bilateral series on Australian soil a memorable one, suffering a seven-wicket defeat to the hosts at Allan Border Field in Brisbane on Friday.
Batting first, Bangladesh were bowled out for 166 in 49.4 overs, a total that proved well below par against the world No. 1 side on home soil.
Australia cruised to 168-3 in just 25.4 overs to take a 1-0 lead in the three-match series.
Amid Bangladesh's disappointing performance, debutant pacer Habiba Islam Pinky offered a glimpse of her potential, claiming 2-36.
She denied Australia a flying start by dismissing opener Georgia Voll for 19, leaving the hosts at 30-1 in the sixth over.
However, it did little to trouble the world's top-ranked team, as Phoebe Litchfield and Ellyse Perry made light work of the chase, sharing an 89-run partnership for the second wicket.
Leg-spinner Rabeya Khan broke the stand by dismissing Litchfield, who smashed 77 off 57 balls, including 10 fours and a six.
Habiba returned to remove Beth Mooney for 13, but Perry and Annabel Sutherland guided Australia home without further trouble.
Perry remained unbeaten on 26, while Sutherland was 25 not out as Australia sealed the victory.
Earlier, Sutherland claimed 4-30 to derail Bangladesh's innings, while Megan Schutt provided able support with 2-19. Ashleigh Gardner, Georgia Wareham and Tahlia McGrath took one wicket apiece.
Bangladesh suffered a poor start after openers Farjana Haque Pinky and Sarmin Sultana were dismissed for single-digit scores.
Captain Nigar Sultana Joty and Sharmin Akter Supta contributed 29 and 24 respectively, but Bangladesh continued to lose wickets at regular intervals.
No. 7 batter Ritu Moni top-scored with 45 off 63 balls to help Bangladesh cross the 150-run mark. However, her effort proved insufficient against one of the most formidable teams in women's cricket.

item.title: Saudi Arabia says three killed at airport as Yemen war expands
item.description:
Saudi Arabia said on Friday that three people were killed including a pilot were killed in attacks on Riyadh’s international airport, after Yemen’s Houthis claimed a series of attacks targeting the facility.
The conflict between the Houthis and Yemen’s Saudi-backed government has widened, with the Iran-backed fighters staging repeated attacks on Saudi targets since they began a lightning offensive just across the border.
While seizing large swathes of territory along the Red Sea coast in Yemen, the Houthis have also attacked Saudi transport hubs, oil facilities and other civilian targets in the world’s largest crude exporter.
The Saudi civil aviation authority said two attacks on Thursday on the Saudi capital’s airport and a Saudia Airlines plane there “resulted in the martyrdom of three citizens.”
The national flag carrier confirmed the death of the plane’s captain, expressing “profound sadness” and citing an “incident” at King Khalid International Airport.
Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government forces it backs have struggled to contain the Houthis’ advance, despite a counter-offensive aimed at recapturing territory including the area around the Bab al-Mandab strait that is crucial to global energy flows.
But a regional source told AFP on Friday that Riyadh would not bow to the Houthis’ “military blackmail” and would not agree to a truce until the Yemeni government regains all territory it has lost in recent weeks.
The attacks forced diplomats stationed in the Saudi capital to shelter in place and international schools to take safety measures, as explosions echoed across the city on Thursday.
Numerous flights at Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport were delayed or cancelled, while the airport advised travelers of the “necessity” to contact airlines before their trips.
The kingdom’s civil defense agency also said “interception debris” had damaged a kindergarten and a medical complex in Riyadh. It did not say if there were casualties there or provide details of the damage.
The Houthis, whose heartlands are among the Zaidi Shia Muslims in the northwest, had already controlled the capital Sanaa and most of Yemen’s major population centers since the start of the war in 2014.
Riyadh’s military coalition intervened to support the government the following year.
After declaring their counter-offensive against the Houthis, Yemen’s government claimed to have pushed the fighters out of strategic areas on the Red Sea coast and the port city of Mocha.
But the Houthis insist they are holding their territory, and military sources from both sides contacted by AFP have not reported any major changes on the ground.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group launched missiles at an airport in Najran and an airbase in Khamis Mushait on Thursday.
The Houthis have also warned workers to evacuate Saudi Arabia’s oil facilities, having days before hit a major refinery south of the capital.
Admissions by Saudi authorities of civilian targets being hit are relatively rare. There have been few statements on Houthi attacks in recent weeks.
Claims by the warring parties have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast and access for journalists difficult.
In Yemen, one of the world’s poorest countries, ordinary civilians are paying the price for the renewed fighting, with more than 200,000 people displaced since July, according to UN data.
In Yemen’s Taiz, the Houthis are laying siege to the government-controlled city in the country’s west, depriving residents of their main supply route to the government’s temporary capital in Aden.
“There is a crisis in everything: water, gas, vegetables, everything essential,” said Um Rian.

item.title: India faces water and power shortages after weak monsoon
item.description:
Ramesh Reddy, 44, put everything he had into his 3.5-acre tomato farm in June. The farmer from Kolar district in the south of the state of Karnataka invested 320,000 rupees, borrowing 250,000 rupees at 24% annual interest and pledging his wife’s wedding jewelry as collateral.
The harvest was meant to repay the loan and cover his son’s overdue college fees. But then the farm’s irrigation well ran dry. Within three weeks, the tomato plants had turned brown and Reddy could not salvage a single crate.
“I have lost everything I invested,” he told DW. “I have no money left for the next crop and I don’t know how I will repay the loan.”
He is now negotiating a job as a security guard in the state capital, Bengaluru, and preparing to leave his farmland behind.
For India, the monsoon is more than just a four-month rainy season. It replenishes reservoirs, supports agriculture and helps sustain water supplies and power generation across much of the country.
Nearly half of India’s workforce depends on farming for their livelihood, doing jobs that are both tough and economically insecure.
This year, the country received 759.4 millimeters of rain between June and September, against a long-term average of 868.6 millimeters. The 12.6% deficit made it the country’s driest monsoon in 11 years and the fourth driest this century.
Madhavan Nair Rajeevan, a climate scientist and former secretary in the Indian Ministry of Earth Sciences, said the main factor behind the poor monsoon was a severe El Nino. He had warned earlier that this global climate phenomenon would pose a serious risk to rainfall.
“As far as the Indian monsoon is concerned, El Nino is the most important influencing factor, which we should consider very seriously,” Rajeevan told DW.
The effects are now hitting India’s water and energy systems. The country’s major reservoirs ended the monsoon with less water than usual, leaving both farmers and the power sector with less of a buffer going into the months ahead.
Combined storage in the 178 reservoirs monitored by the Central Water Commission stood at 132.7 billion cubic meters, below the 10-year average of 151.1 billion cubic meters.
That shortfall is already being felt in electricity generation. Hydropower output fell nearly 16% in September from a year earlier, according to Grid India data. At the same time, electricity shortages reached 560 million kilowatt-hours, the highest monthly shortfall in more than three years. After sunset, when solar generation drops off, the grid has fewer options to make up the difference.
Coal-fired plants have, therefore, had to shoulder more of the load, but they face a problem of their own. Data from the Central Electricity Authority showed that around 40% of coal-fired plants had critically low stocks, with supplies below a quarter of the required level.
The government has ordered some private industrial power plants to operate at full capacity and feed surplus electricity into the grid.
Manufacturers are already feeling the strain. “Uninterrupted power supply is of paramount importance for manufacturing units, as power cuts disrupt production cycles,” said Ashok Gupta, the president of the Mohali Industries Association, which represents nearly 600 small and medium-sized manufacturers.
“Such disruptions not only cause losses to manufacturers but also result in wastage of raw materials.”
The economic impact of a poor monsoon can extend well beyond agriculture. Weaker farm output can hit rural incomes, employment and consumption, while higher food prices put further pressure on household budgets.
Arun Kumar, a retired professor of economics, said the effects could be wider than the headline economic numbers suggest, particularly because much of India’s rural economy operates outside the formal sector.
“Economic development needs to be assessed through a wider set of indicators,” Kumar told DW. He said weaker agricultural output could push up food prices while putting pressure on incomes and consumption.
Himanshu, a development economist at Delhi’s Jawaharlal Nehru University, described the situation as a “twin shock” for rural households, with weaker farm incomes coming alongside higher food prices.
“When agricultural incomes fall and food prices rise, rural households face a squeeze on their purchasing power,” he told DW.
The economist said that the uneven distribution of rainfall could compound the problem, with some farming regions suffering much heavier losses than the national rainfall figure indicates. “The impact on rural consumption could also be significant, as households facing lower incomes and higher food costs have less money to spend on other goods and services.”
The pressure is also being felt in urban households. A survey in September by India’s central bank found that households were expecting inflation to rise as food and fuel prices increasingly affected sentiment.
Sunita Sharma, a homemaker in New Delhi, said her usual shopping list now costs hundreds of rupees more than it did a few months ago.
“We have no option but to cut down on discretionary expenses just to afford basic, everyday meals,” she told DW.
The prices of some staples have risen sharply recently. An analysis by ISignal using Department of Consumer Affairs data found that onions were 93% more expensive in September than a year earlier, while sugar prices rose by 28% and rice by about 8%.
The next test will be the rabi, or winter, crop. Farmers are now preparing to plant wheat, mustard and chickpeas, but success will depend largely on how much moisture remains in the soil after the weak monsoon.
Rajeevan said the longer-term outlook was also becoming increasingly difficult to predict as the climate warms.
“In a warming climate, longer dry spells and greater rainfall variability is a possibility,” he said. “In future, in addition to the influence of El Nino events, we should expect the influence of a warmer climate.”
Reddy, the farmer in Karnataka state, is now waiting to hear whether he has got the security job in Bengaluru, and preparing to leave his farm behind.

item.title: France students plan more protests, UN ‘concerned’ over violence
item.description:
Students in France were largely back in the classroom Friday following days of protests demanding better education, with the UN voicing “concern” over the sometimes violent clashes.
Tens of thousands have taken to the streets across France since students in late September began blocking entrances to high schools, which in turn saw squads of riot police deployed.
The students -- most aged 15 to 18 -- have complained of absent teachers, overloaded timetables, dilapidated classrooms and buildings that cannot cope with rising temperatures.
More than 6,800 people have been detained since the start of the demonstrations, of whom 86 percent are minors, the justice ministry said Friday.
The United Nations said Friday it was watching the events “with concern” and urging people on all sides to remain peaceful.
“We are following with concern incidents related to the student protests and high school blockades in France, some of which have turned violent,” said Shabia Mantoo, spokesperson for the UN human rights agency.
While the demonstrations have been largely peaceful, some protesters have started fires and vandalized bus shelters.
In response, police have used tear gas, batons and blast balls, leading to accusations from rights groups and the children of a disproportionate use of force.
Police have opened 18 internal investigations into allegations of misconduct.
A 15-year-old lost a hand on Monday after police fired a stun grenade, and the government has suspended the use of the weapon.
On Thursday evening in the capital Paris, police said they used tear gas in Bastille square to disperse some “high-risk profiles.”
In a bid to placate the anger, Education Minister Edouard Geffray announced late Thursday that some 3,000 substitute teachers would be deployed in the coming days to replace absent staff at the 114 worst-affected high schools.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has also promised a plan to respond to the crisis by the end of October, while Economy Minister Roland Lescure said there was room to address demands for more school resources within the highly constrained 2027 budget.
In the current draft budget, education has the second largest increase in funding -- after defense -- with a boost of 1.4% to 90.9 billion euros.
Of the 3,700 high schools across France, called lycées, only 141 were closed on Friday, the education ministry reported.
Last Friday, some 800 schools had closed due to the protests.
But many students told AFP they were not relenting, with organizers calling for large-scale demonstrations next week.
“We’re saving our energy for next week,” said one 16-year-old student in Toulouse.
Alice, a high school student in Marseille, said the education minister’s announcements “are a first step but they’re not enough.”
Student union representative Marius Mesnil said “we’re being offered a few crumbs,” while calling for another wave of demonstrations Tuesday.

item.title: India deploys thousands of police ahead of election protest
item.description:
Thousands of police were deployed across the Indian capital on Friday, a day before planned protests to demand the election commission chief step down over alleged voter-roll irregularities.
Demonstrations have erupted this month over the Election Commission of India’s (ECI) “special intensive revision” of electoral rolls, which the commission says is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible voters.
Opposition parties and critics allege the exercise could disenfranchise voters to the benefit of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
A wave of street protests, including in New Delhi, has attracted key leaders from India’s main opposition Congress party, including Rahul Gandhi, who was briefly detained during rallies this week.
Protesters, including from the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) movement, are calling for mass rallies in New Delhi on Saturday.
Gandhi, the leader of the opposition in parliament, and other opposition leaders are expected to meet President Droupadi Murmu later Friday to complain about ECI chief Gyanesh Kumar.
The ECI, India’s constitutional body responsible for conducting elections, has rejected allegations of wrongdoing.
More than 20,000 police and paramilitary officers have been deployed in the capital ahead of the protest, the Press Trust of India news agency reported.
Yellow metal barricades have sprung up across key roads in the city center, restricting access to the government-designated protest site of Jantar Mantar, AFP reporters saw.
Police have not authorized rallies at the site, and ordered the Delhi Metro subway system to close entry and exit gates at some stations from late Friday, according to media reports.
“In view of proposed protests and the likelihood of unruly mob movement, Delhi Metro entry/exit gates across 57 stations may be closed from 9:00 PM IST on October 9 till the situation normalizes on October 10,” a police letter to the metro operator said.
Authorities have also cancelled several incoming trains at two key train stations in the city for Saturday, according to local reports.
The Cockroach Janta Party emerged online in May as a satirical political movement, and led protests at Jantar Mantar -- which succeeded in a campaign to oust the then education minister.
The CJP has called for a “mass mobilization” in New Delhi on Saturday, including an intended march to Jantar Mantar.
The movement has claimed that its volunteers and supporters were being detained by police ahead of the planned demonstration -- allegations police did not respond to.
“Delhi police is working like the BJP’s private militia,” CJP activist Saurav Das said in a post on social media.
CJP chief Abhijeet Dipke said on social media on Friday that “this intimidation is not going to work, Modi.”
“The youth of this country are no longer scared of you,” Dipke added.
“I’ll be landing in Delhi tomorrow and will march to Jantar Mantar, come what may.”

item.title: ‘Mental health awareness remains a major challenge’
item.description:
On the occasion of World Mental Health Day, Professor Dr Saifun Nahar, director of the National Institute of Mental Health and Hospital, spoke to Dhaka Tribune about Bangladesh’s mental health situation, healthcare services, social stigma, mental health among children and adolescents, and suicide prevention.
Dr Saifun Nahar: According to the National Mental Health Survey 2019, the prevalence of mental health problems among adults in Bangladesh is 18.7%, while the rate among children and adolescents is 12.6%. Among people aged 60 and above, 28% experience mental health problems.
Patients with various mental health conditions visit our outpatient and inpatient departments, where we provide treatment for almost all types of mental health problems.
Among children, online gaming addiction, gambling-related problems, internet addiction and mobile phone addiction are becoming increasingly common.
There are different types of mental health problems, which can broadly be classified into neurotic and psychotic disorders. Changes in brain functioning can affect a person's thoughts, emotions, behaviour and daily life.
As a result, their ability to function in their personal, professional, family and social lives may deteriorate. In general, changes in one's daily activities and functioning can help indicate a potential problem.
A mentally healthy person can generally maintain normal functioning and productivity in their work, communication, social interactions and other activities. Significant changes in these areas, however, may indicate a mental health problem.
Many people with psychotic disorders have limited awareness of their condition, and their judgement may also become impaired. Consequently, they may not recognise the need for treatment.
People experiencing neurotic disorders, on the other hand, can often identify changes in themselves. These may include mood swings, a loss of interest in routine activities, difficulty completing tasks or a decline in the quality of their work.
Mental health problems can also manifest as physical symptoms, including loss of appetite, headaches, body aches and digestive problems. They may also affect sexual desire or functioning.
The mind and body are closely connected, and mental health problems can also affect physical health. For example, many patients with depression experience various physical aches and pains. Anxiety-related disorders can cause palpitations, digestive problems and headaches.
Anyone experiencing a mental health problem should seek medical attention. However, when relatives or neighbours learn that someone is receiving mental health treatment, the person may sometimes face social humiliation. We must move away from these superstitions and prejudices. Unless we break this taboo, we will not be able to address the problem effectively.
There are also many misconceptions about mental health. Some people believe that counselling alone is enough to ensure recovery, that medication must be taken for life once treatment begins, that mental illnesses are incurable, or that psychiatric medication damages the brain. We must work to dispel these misconceptions.
Patients can recover with appropriate treatment and medication taken as prescribed by a doctor. We must also strengthen public trust in doctors and mental health services.
More than 500 patients visit our outpatient department every day. Our inpatient department has 400 beds. At times, all the beds are occupied, while on other occasions, occupancy is around 80%.
We are working to improve our services further. The current government is also taking initiatives to advance mental health services.
Our mental health workforce is still inadequate. However, compared with the past, more talented students are choosing to study this subject. We have introduced four additional courses in response to growing interest in the field. At the same time, the workforce is gradually expanding.
Children experience different types of mental health problems depending on their age. Among children and adolescents, we see cases of autism spectrum disorder, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), internet addiction, gaming addiction and mobile phone addiction.
Many children are also developing problematic patterns of pornography use. Drug addiction is another concern among street children, with some becoming increasingly involved in glue sniffing and the use of readily available drugs such as yaba.
A coordinated approach is needed to address mental health problems among children and adolescents. Conflict and other forms of pressure within the family can affect a child's mental well-being. When children regularly witness arguments between their parents, their cognitive development may be affected, and they may develop trust issues later in life.
If they struggle to manage anger and stress, they may also become vulnerable to suicidal thoughts or behaviour.
Similarly, children who experience bullying or humiliation at school, or face excessive academic pressure, may develop various mental health problems that can affect them later in life.
People with certain personality disorders, particularly those with abrasive personality traits, may exhibit suicidal behaviour. People living with various mental illnesses, including those experiencing hallucinations or delusions, may also develop suicidal tendencies. Drug addiction can also increase the risk of suicide.
Awareness is crucial in this regard. Suicide can be prevented by identifying mental health problems early and ensuring that those affected receive appropriate treatment and support.
Mental health services have expanded compared with the situation 10 years ago. Through the World Health Organization's mental health programme, doctors from different districts and upazilas are receiving training to help reduce gaps in treatment services.
Doctors from areas outside major urban centres are brought in for training. After returning to their respective workplaces, they pass on their knowledge and train other healthcare professionals.
There may not be dedicated posts for psychiatrists at district- or upazila-level health complexes. However, doctors working in these areas are being trained to provide primary mental healthcare to patients. After completing their training, they return to their respective areas and provide services there.
Regardless of the cause of an illness, anyone who is unwell should receive appropriate treatment. Whether mental health problems stem from personal circumstances, family issues or other factors, seeking treatment is essential.
Sometimes, people do not realise that they are experiencing a mental health problem. In such cases, family members and relatives should help them seek professional care by taking them to a psychiatrist and arranging the necessary counselling or other treatment.
The government has already undertaken various projects to strengthen community mental health teams. The integration of mental health services into primary healthcare was included in earlier initiatives, and the programme is now being advanced further.
One year is a very short time, and it is not possible to resolve all the challenges within that period. The treatment gap remains substantial. Among adults, it is 92%, while among children, it is 95%.
This means that only 8% of adults who need mental health services are receiving them, while the remaining 92% are not. Among children who need such services, only 5% receive them, leaving 95% without access to the care they need.
If everyone works together, we can bring about positive changes. However, resolving all these problems within a single year is not possible. We are continuing our efforts to improve the situation.
Public awareness remains inadequate, and many people do not give mental health the importance it deserves. Much of the problem can be addressed if people take mental illness seriously and seek treatment when necessary.
Individuals, families, educational institutions and the state must all work together to raise awareness, reduce stigma and ensure that people with mental health conditions receive appropriate care.

item.title: Four arrested with firearms in Chittagong’s Jungle Salimpur
item.description:
Police arrested four alleged terrorists along with firearms, ammunition, and domestic weapons during a special operation in the remote hilly terrain of Jungle Salimpur in Sitakunda upazila of Chittagong.
District police conducted the drive on Thursday in the Alinagar Bahadur Ghona area of Jungle Salimpur based on secret intelligence. Details of the raid were disclosed by Additional Superintendent of Police Junaid Kawsar during a press conference at Sitakunda Model Police Station on Friday noon.
The arrested individuals were identified as Md Russel, Md Morshed, Mohammad Babu, and Md Sabbir. All four are accused in multiple robbery and terrorism cases and have long been involved in extortion and criminal activities, police said.
During the drive, police recovered a foreign Chinese pistol, a shotgun, six lead cartridges, nine rounds of bullets, a spear (teda), a machete (chapati), an iron cutter, and a handwritten list used for collecting extortion money.
"Conducting drives in Jungle Salimpur is challenging due to its vast hilly area, dense jungle, and difficult communication system," Additional SP Junaid Kawsar said. "Overcoming the adverse topography, officers identified the target based on intelligence and conducted the operation with caution and strategy, leading to the arrest of the four individuals."
